objectives: Reduce a three-value search to a two-pointer search by fixing one value.
Count or find triples in O(n²) instead of O(n³).
Explain which pointer to move and why no answer is skipped.

sections.heading: Intuition: fix one value, solve the pair problem
paragraphs: Three nested loops over an array try every triple: O(n³). But once you fix the first value, the rest is a pair problem, and day 15 solved pair problems on sorted arrays in one pass. So sort, loop over the first value, and run two pointers on the values after it: O(n²).
The two pointers only work if moving one of them provably can't skip an answer. That argument is the part to get right on every problem this week.

callout.text: When you move a pointer, finish the sentence "every pair using the value I'm leaving has already been handled because ...". If you can't, the move may skip an answer.

diagram.description: Sorted values -2, 0, 1, 3. The first value is fixed; lo and hi scan the values after it.

sections.heading: Baseline: try every triple
paragraphs: Three loops with i < j < k check every triple once. It's correct, easy to test against, and O(n³): a thousand values means about 166 million triples.

sections.heading: Worked example: count triples with a small sum
paragraphs: Count triples i < lo < hi whose sum is less than a target. Sort first. For each i, set lo = i + 1 and hi = n - 1.

If the triple's sum is below the target, then replacing values[hi] with anything between lo and hi gives a smaller sum, so all hi - lo triples with this i and lo count. Add them and move lo right. Otherwise values[hi] is too big with every remaining partner, so move hi left.
For [-2, 0, 1, 3] and target 2, fixing -2 finds (-2, 0, 1) and (-2, 0, 3). Fixing 0 finds nothing. The answer is 2.

sections.heading: Your turn: 3Sum
paragraphs: Today's first medium. Return every distinct triple of values that sums to 0. The answer must not contain the same triple twice, even if the input has repeated values.

callout.text: The counting example handles the pointers. The new part is duplicates: run it on [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4] by hand and see where the same triple would be found twice.
callout.title: Where to start

sections.heading: Your turn: 3Sum Closest
paragraphs: Today's second medium. Return the sum of three values that is closest to target. Exactly one answer exists.

callout.text: You're no longer counting or matching exactly. What do you record at each step, and does the pointer rule still work when the sum equals the target?
callout.title: Where to start

sections.navLabel: Your turn: Container With Most Water
sections.heading: Your turn: Container With Most Water
paragraphs: Today's third medium. Each value is the height of a vertical line. Pick two lines; together with the x-axis they hold water, limited by the shorter line. Return the most water any pair can hold.

callout.text: Start with the widest pair. Moving a pointer inward always loses width. Which pointer's move could possibly gain enough height to make up for it?
callout.title: Where to start

sections.heading: Complexity and cautions
paragraphs: Fixing one value and scanning with two pointers is O(n²) after an O(n log n) sort, with O(1) extra memory besides the output.
Sums of three values can overflow 32-bit integers when inputs are large. Check the problem's limits and use 64-bit math if needed.

sections.heading: Before you finish
paragraphs: Try to answer each question before opening it.

checks.prompt: Why does sorting make the two-pointer step work?
checks.answer: It makes the sum grow when lo moves right and shrink when hi moves left, so each comparison tells you which end to drop.

checks.prompt: In the counting example, why can hi - lo triples be counted at once?
checks.answer: Every value between lo and hi is at most values[hi], so each of those triples also has a small enough sum.

checks.prompt: What does fixing the first value turn the problem into?
checks.answer: A pair problem on the values after it, which two pointers solve in one pass.
